title: Unit 7: Oscillations

topics.name: Periodic motion and simple harmonic motion

guide.title: Oscillations: review guide
guide.intro: Many systems move back and forth around a stable equilibrium. When the restoring force or torque is proportional to the displacement, the motion is simple harmonic, and its period does not depend on the amplitude.
guide.equationNote: g = 10 m/s² unless stated. Use radians: ω is in rad/s.

sections.title: Periodic motion and simple harmonic motion
body: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) happens when the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, F = −kx. Newton's second law gives d²x/dt² = −(k/m)x, whose solution is x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ) with ω = √(k/m).
The period is T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k), and the frequency is f = 1/T. The speed is greatest at equilibrium, v_max = Aω, and the acceleration is greatest at the turning points, a_max = Aω².
points: Any equation of the form d²x/dt² = −Cx describes SHM with ω = √C.
Energy: ½kA² = ½mv² + ½kx² at every point of the motion.
The period of an ideal mass–spring system does not depend on the amplitude.

sections.title: Simple pendulums
body: A simple pendulum is a small mass on a light string of length L. For small angles sin θ ≈ θ, so the restoring torque is proportional to θ and the motion is approximately SHM.
Its period is T = 2π√(L/g). It does not depend on the mass, and for small swings it does not depend on the amplitude.
points: Four times the length doubles the period.
Weaker gravity, as on the Moon, makes the period longer.
For large amplitudes the period is a little longer than the formula predicts.

sections.title: Physical pendulums
body: A physical pendulum is any rigid object swinging about a pivot. Gravity acts at the center of mass, a distance d from the pivot, giving a restoring torque −mgd sin θ ≈ −mgdθ for small angles.
Using Στ = Iα with I measured about the pivot gives ω = √(mgd/I) and T = 2π√(I/(mgd)). A simple pendulum is the special case I = mL², d = L.
points: Use the parallel-axis theorem to find I about the pivot.
For a uniform rod pivoted at one end, I = (1/3)mL² and d = L/2, so T = 2π√(2L/(3g)).
The mass cancels for a given shape; the shape and the pivot's location set the period.

example.prompt: A 0.40 kg mass on a spring with k = 160 N/m is pulled 0.050 m from equilibrium and released. Find the period, the maximum speed, and the total energy.

misconceptions: A simple pendulum's period does not depend on its mass.
“A bigger amplitude means a longer period.”
In SHM the period does not depend on the amplitude (for a pendulum, as long as the angle stays small).
“At the turning points the acceleration is zero.”
There v = 0, but the acceleration is at its largest.
“A physical pendulum acts like a simple pendulum of the same length.”
Its period depends on its rotational inertia about the pivot and the distance to its center of mass.

questions.prompt: A 0.50 kg mass on a spring with k = 50 N/m oscillates. What is its period?
choiceExplanations: 0.10 s is √(m/k); the factor 2π is missing.
63 s uses √(k/m), the ratio upside down.
1.6 is 1/T, the frequency in hertz, not the period.

questions.prompt: An object's position is x(t) = 0.20 cos(5t) meters. What is its maximum speed?
choiceExplanations: 5.0 is Aω², the maximum acceleration in m/s².
0.20 m is the amplitude, a distance.
0.040 is A/ω; the derivative multiplies by ω.

questions.prompt: A mass on a spring with k = 200 N/m oscillates with an amplitude of 0.10 m. What is its kinetic energy when it is 0.050 m from equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Total energy ½kA² = ½(200)(0.10)² = 1.0 J. At x = 0.050 m the spring stores ½(200)(0.050)² = 0.25 J, so K = 1.0 − 0.25 = 0.75 J.
choiceExplanations: 0.50 J assumes the energy splits evenly at half the amplitude, but spring energy depends on x².
0.25 J is the spring's potential energy at that point.
1.0 J is the total energy, which is all kinetic only at equilibrium.

questions.prompt: An object's motion obeys d²x/dt² = −16x, in SI units. What is the period of its oscillation?
questions.explanation: Compare with d²x/dt² = −ω²x: ω² = 16, so ω = 4.0 rad/s and T = 2π/ω ≈ 1.6 s.
choiceExplanations: 0.39 s is 2π/16, which treats 16 as ω instead of ω².
0.25 is 1/ω; the period is 2π/ω.
4.0 is ω, the angular frequency in rad/s.

questions.prompt: What is the period of a simple pendulum 2.5 m long, swinging through small angles? (g = 10 m/s²)
choiceExplanations: 0.50 s is √(L/g); the factor 2π is missing.
12.6 s uses √(g/L), the ratio upside down.
0.25 is L/g; the period uses its square root, times 2π.

questions.prompt: A simple pendulum's length is made four times as long and its bob's mass is doubled. What happens to its period (for small swings)?
choices: It becomes four times as long
It becomes about 2.8 times as long
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g) depends on the length but not the mass. Four times the length gives √4 = 2 times the period.
choiceExplanations: The period depends on √L, so four times the length doubles it rather than quadrupling it.
2.8 ≈ 2√2 wrongly lets the doubled mass change the period too; the mass has no effect.
The length changed, and the period depends on the length.

questions.prompt: A pendulum clock is taken to the Moon, where gravity is about one sixth as strong as on Earth. How does its pendulum's period change?
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(L/g), so dividing g by 6 multiplies T by √6 ≈ 2.4. The clock runs slow.
choiceExplanations: The period depends on 1/√g, so it grows by √6, not by 6.
Weaker gravity gives a weaker restoring force, so the swing is slower and the period longer.
The period depends on g, so it changes.

questions.prompt: A uniform rod 1.5 m long swings about a pivot at one end through small angles. What is its period? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: For a rod pivoted at one end, I = (1/3)mL² and d = L/2, so T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) = 2π√(2L/(3g)) = 2π√(0.10) ≈ 2.0 s.
choiceExplanations: 2.4 s treats the rod as a simple pendulum 1.5 m long, as if all its mass were at the end.
1.7 s treats it as a simple pendulum of length L/2, which leaves out the rod's rotational inertia.
1.0 s uses I = (1/12)mL², the value about the rod's center, without the parallel-axis term.

questions.prompt: For small swings, which quantities set the period of a physical pendulum?
choices: Its rotational inertia about the pivot and the distance from the pivot to its center of mass, but not the size of the swing
Only its total length, as for a simple pendulum
Only its mass: a heavier object swings faster
Only how far it is pulled back before release
questions.explanation: T = 2π√(I/(mgd)). It depends on I about the pivot and on d (with the mass canceling for a given shape), not on the amplitude when the angles are small.
choiceExplanations: Two objects of the same length can have different rotational inertias and centers of mass, so they swing with different periods.
For a given shape, I is proportional to m, so the mass cancels in I/(mgd).
For small angles the period does not depend on the amplitude.

questions.prompt: A pendulum is released from a large angle, 60°, instead of a small one. How does its actual period compare with the small-angle formula?
choices: It is somewhat longer, because the restoring torque is proportional to sin θ, which is less than θ
It is exactly the same, because the period never depends on the amplitude
It is shorter, because the pendulum has farther to fall and so moves faster
It is twice as long, because the angle is doubled
questions.explanation: The formula assumes sin θ ≈ θ. At large angles sin θ < θ, so the restoring torque is weaker than the linear model predicts, and the pendulum takes longer to complete each swing.
choiceExplanations: Amplitude independence is exact only for true SHM; a pendulum is SHM only in the small-angle approximation.
It does move faster at the bottom, but it travels farther, and the weaker-than-linear restoring torque makes each swing take longer overall.
The period grows only slightly at 60° (by roughly 7%); it does not double.
